```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(mixvlmc)
```

This article describes how to represent context trees, variable length Markov
chains (VLMC) and VLMC with covariates as trees, using the `draw()` function.
`draw()` produces either an "ascii art" representation, well suited to the R
console, or a LaTeX representation of the tree, to be included in a LaTeX
document or in an R Markdown or Quarto document that produces a PDF.

`draw()` is a generic function with methods for the three types of objects:
`draw.ctx_tree()` for context trees, `draw.vlmc()` for VLMC and `draw.covlmc()`
for VLMC with covariates. Context trees and VLMC are drawn in the same way
whatever their backend (the default C++ backend or the R one, see `ctx_tree()`
and `vlmc()`). All the methods share the same organisation:

- the `format` argument (the second one) selects the output format, either
  `"text"` (the default) or `"latex"`;
- additional arguments specific to each method specify *what* information is
  shown in each node of the tree (frequencies, probabilities, models, etc.);
- the `control` argument, built with `draw_control()`, specifies *how* this
  information is shown (characters used to draw the tree, number of significant
  digits, LaTeX layout, etc.).

This organisation of the arguments was introduced in mixvlmc 0.3.0. Calls
written for previous versions, in which the second argument of `draw()` was
the control list, still work but trigger a deprecation warning.

The models used in this article are kept very simple: see
`vignette("context-trees")`, `vignette("variable-length-markov-chains")` and
`vignette("covlmc")` for the construction and the interpretation of context
trees and models.

## Context trees

### Basic representation

We use a small random sequence on three states.

```{r}
set.seed(0)
x <- sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 100, replace = TRUE)
x_ctx <- ctx_tree(x, min_size = 10, max_depth = 2)
draw(x_ctx)
```

The root of the tree (the empty context) is shown by a small square. Each node
of the first level corresponds to the most recent state of a context
($x_{t-1}$), each node of the second level to the state before it ($x_{t-2}$),
etc. A context is therefore read from its node to the root in chronological
order. For instance, the leaf `b` under the node `a` stands for the context in
which `b` is followed by `a`, denoted `b, a` by `contexts()`:

```{r}
contexts(x_ctx)
```

### Frequencies

The `frequency` argument of `draw.ctx_tree()` adds the frequencies of the
(partial) contexts to the representation. With `frequency = "total"`, each node
shows the number of occurrences of its context in the sequence (only the
occurrences followed by at least one state are taken into account, see
`vignette("context-trees")`).

```{r}
draw(x_ctx, frequency = "total")
```

With `frequency = "detailed"`, each node shows the number of occurrences of
each state that follows its context, in the order of the state space given by
`states()` (here `r paste(states(x_ctx), collapse = ", ")`).

```{r}
draw(x_ctx, frequency = "detailed")
```

This is the same information as the one given by `contexts()` with the same
`frequency` argument, organised as a tree.

## Variable length Markov chains

### Probabilities and frequencies

Each context of a VLMC is associated with a conditional distribution of the
next state. `draw.vlmc()` shows those distributions by default. We use as an
example a VLMC fitted to a discretised version of the active power of week 5
of the household electricity consumption data set (`powerconsumption`). The
model is selected with the BIC (see `vignette("variable-length-markov-chains")`
and `vignette("model-selection")`).

```{r}
pc_week_5 <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week == 5, ]
elec_dts <- cut(pc_week_5$active_power,
  breaks = c(0, 0.4, 2, 8),
  labels = c("low", "typical", "high")
)
elec_vlmc <- as_vlmc(tune_vlmc(elec_dts))
draw(elec_vlmc)
```

The probabilities are given in the order of the state space, here:

```{r}
states(elec_vlmc)
```

The root node gives the marginal distribution of the states in the sequence,
while the other nodes give the distribution of the next state conditionally on
their (partial) context.

The `prob` argument controls this display: `prob = FALSE` replaces the
probabilities by the frequencies of the states that follow each (partial)
context (as `frequency = "detailed"` in `draw.ctx_tree()`), while
`prob = NULL` removes all the information.

```{r}
draw(elec_vlmc, prob = FALSE)
draw(elec_vlmc, prob = NULL)
```

### Number of digits

Probabilities (and other numerical values) are rounded with `signif()` to the
number of significant digits given by the `digits` parameter of
`draw_control()` (4 by default).

```{r}
draw(elec_vlmc, control = draw_control(digits = 2))
```

## Text representations

### Character sets

The "ascii art" representation uses a collection of characters, the *charset*,
to draw the branches of the tree and to delimit the information attached to
the nodes. The package provides two charsets:

- `"utf8"`: the charset returned by `charset_utf8()`, based on UTF-8 symbols
  (used in this article);
- `"ascii"`: the charset returned by `charset_ascii()`, based on standard ASCII
  characters only.

The default charset is given by the `mixvlmc.charset` option. When the package
is loaded, this option is set to `"utf8"` if the output supports UTF-8
characters (according to `cli::is_utf8_output()`) and to `"ascii"` otherwise
(unless the option was already set). The charset can be changed for a single
call with the `charset` parameter of `draw_control()`:

```{r}
draw(x_ctx, control = draw_control(charset = "ascii"))
```

or for all subsequent calls by setting the option:

```{r}
options(mixvlmc.charset = "ascii")
draw(x_ctx, frequency = "total")
options(mixvlmc.charset = "utf8")
```

### Custom charsets

`charset_utf8()` and `charset_ascii()` return lists of character strings, one
per element of the representation. All their arguments can be modified to
obtain a custom charset, which is then given to `draw_control()`:

```{r}
str(charset_ascii())
```

The first elements are used for all the trees:

- `root`: the symbol of the root node;
- `first_node`, `next_node` and `final_node`: the symbols that introduce the
  first child of a node, its intermediate children and its last child;
- `vbranch` and `hbranch`: the vertical and horizontal parts of the branches;
- `open_ct` and `close_ct`: the delimiters of the information attached to a
  node (frequencies, probabilities, models).

For instance:

```{r}
my_charset <- charset_ascii(
  root = "@",
  final_node = "+",
  hbranch = "==",
  open_ct = "<",
  close_ct = ">"
)
draw(x_ctx,
  frequency = "detailed",
  control = draw_control(charset = my_charset)
)
```

The other elements (`level_sep`, `time_sep`, `intercept`, `intercept_sep`,
`open_p_value`, `close_p_value`, `open_model` and `close_model`) are used only
by `draw.covlmc()` and are described below.

## VLMC with covariates

### A two-state model

A VLMC with covariates (see `vignette("covlmc")`) associates to each context a
logistic model that gives the conditional distribution of the next state as a
function of past values of the covariates. `draw.covlmc()` represents those
models in the tree. We start with a two-state sequence and a single logical
covariate.

```{r}
elec_dts_2 <- cut(pc_week_5$active_power,
  breaks = c(0, median(pc_week_5$active_power), 8),
  labels = c("low", "high")
)
elec_cov <- data.frame(day = (pc_week_5$hour >= 7 & pc_week_5$hour <= 17))
elec_covlmc <- covlmc(elec_dts_2, elec_cov, min_size = 5)
draw(elec_covlmc)
```

Two types of models appear in the tree:

- *constant models* do not depend on the covariates. By default, they are
  represented by the conditional distribution of the next state that they
  induce, as for a VLMC (in the order of `states(elec_covlmc)`);
- other models are represented between brackets by their coefficients. With a
  logistic model, the coefficients describe the logarithm of the ratio between
  the probability of the second state (here `high`) and the probability of the
  first state (here `low`, the *reference* state). The intercept comes first,
  followed by the coefficients of the covariates at time $t-1$, then at time
  $t-2$, etc. The intercept is separated from the other coefficients by the
  `intercept_sep` element of the charset (a bullet with UTF-8 characters) and
  consecutive time steps are separated by the `time_sep` element (a vertical
  dotted line with UTF-8 characters).

For instance, the model of the context made of three consecutive `low` states
(the deepest `low` leaf) has an intercept followed by one coefficient for each
of the values of `day` at times $t-1$, $t-2$ and $t-3$, while the model of its
sibling `high` only uses the value of `day` at time $t-1$.

Setting `constant_as_prob = FALSE` represents constant models by their
coefficients, that is by their intercept only:

```{r}
draw(elec_covlmc, constant_as_prob = FALSE)
```

The probabilities shown in the default representation are obtained from the
intercepts with the logistic function. With `model = "full"`, the names of the
variables are shown above the coefficients (and constant models are always
represented by their coefficients):

```{r}
draw(elec_covlmc, model = "full")
```

The names of the variables are generated by the underlying logistic model and
include the time delay: for instance `day_1TRUE` stands for the value `TRUE` of
the covariate `day` at time $t-1$. The intercept is denoted by the `intercept`
element of the charset (`(I)` by default).

With `with_state = TRUE`, each row of coefficients is preceded by the state it
predicts. With `model = "coef"` (the default), the state is followed by the
reference state, while with `model = "full"` the reference state is shown, in
parentheses, on the row of the variable names. States are separated from the
coefficients by the `level_sep` element of the charset. Constant models
represented by probabilities are not modified.

```{r}
draw(elec_covlmc, with_state = TRUE)
draw(elec_covlmc, model = "full", with_state = TRUE)
```

This option is particularly useful when some states never follow a context:
they are then removed from its logistic model, which has fewer rows of
coefficients than expected (see examples in `vignette("covlmc")` and in the
article on [computing engines](covlmc-engines.html)).

### More states and covariates

With more than two states, the logistic models have one row of coefficients
for each state but the reference one. Moreover, each time step can be
associated with several coefficients: a numerical or logical covariate has one
coefficient per time step, while a factor has one coefficient per level, except
the first one. We illustrate this with a simulated sequence on three states and
a factor covariate with three levels.

```{r}
set.seed(0)
z <- sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 1000, replace = TRUE)
y <- ifelse(runif(length(z)) > 0.5,
  c(z[-1], sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 1)),
  c(z[-c(1, 2)], sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 2, replace = TRUE))
)
y <- as.factor(ifelse(runif(length(z)) > 0.2, y,
  sample(c("A", "B", "C"), length(z), replace = TRUE)
))
z_covlmc <- covlmc(z, data.frame(y = y), min_size = 1.5, alpha = 0.01)
draw(z_covlmc, model = "full", with_state = TRUE)
```

In this representation, `y_1B` and `y_1C` stand for the levels `B` and `C` of
the covariate `y` at time $t-1$, while `y_2B` and `y_2C` stand for the same
levels at time $t-2$, etc.

The tree also shows a *merged* context: the leaf labelled `A, B` under the
node `B` of the second level represents the two contexts `A, B, B` and
`B, B, B` (in chronological order), which share a single logistic model. The
fitting algorithm of `covlmc()` merges contexts in this way when their models
are not significantly different (see `vignette("covlmc")`, and
`vignette("dts-and-contexts")` for the exploration of merged contexts).

### p-values

During the construction of the model, `covlmc()` conducts a series of
likelihood ratio tests. Their p-values are included in the representation when
`p_value = TRUE`:

```{r}
draw(z_covlmc, p_value = TRUE)
```

The p-value attached to a model, shown between the `open_p_value` and
`close_p_value` delimiters of the charset, is associated with the test that
compares the model to a model with a shorter memory of the covariates. Internal
nodes can show p-values associated with the merging of some of their children
(`merging`) or with the removal of all their children (`collapsing`), as
explained in `vignette("covlmc")`. The models can be removed from the
representation with `model = NULL`, which gives a compact view of the
p-values:

```{r}
draw(z_covlmc, model = NULL, p_value = TRUE)
```

### Customising the model representation

The elements of the charset dedicated to `draw.covlmc()` can be modified as
the other ones. For instance, the following charset uses `+` between the
intercept and the other coefficients, `;` between time steps, `:` between the
states and the coefficients, and braces around the models:

```{r}
cov_charset <- charset_utf8(
  intercept_sep = " + ",
  time_sep = " ; ",
  level_sep = " : ",
  open_model = "{",
  close_model = "}"
)
draw(elec_covlmc,
  model = "full", with_state = TRUE,
  control = draw_control(charset = cov_charset, digits = 3)
)
```

## The result of `draw()`

`draw()` does not print anything by itself: it returns an object of class
`mixvlmc_draw` that contains the representation of the tree, one line per
element.

```{r}
x_draw <- draw(x_ctx)
class(x_draw)
```

As for other R objects, this object is printed automatically when the result
of `draw()` is not assigned to a variable at top level, which is why calling
`draw(x_ctx)` in the console (or in a chunk of an R Markdown document) displays
the tree. Inside a function or a loop, automatic printing does not happen and
the representation must be printed explicitly with `print()`:

```{r}
for (depth in 1:2) {
  print(draw(ctx_tree(x, min_size = 10, max_depth = depth)))
}
```

The lines of the representation are obtained as a character vector with
`format()` or `as.character()`:

```{r}
as.character(x_draw)
```

They can be written to a file with `writeLines()`, for instance to include a
LaTeX representation in a document (see below):

```{r}
tree_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".tex")
writeLines(format(draw(x_ctx, "latex")), tree_file)
```

## LaTeX representations

### The forest package

With `format = "latex"`, `draw()` produces LaTeX code based on the
[forest](https://ctan.org/pkg/forest) LaTeX package. Each call produces a
complete `forest` environment in which each node is described between square
brackets, the children of a node being nested in its description. The root of
the tree is represented by $\epsilon$ (the empty context). In this HTML
article, the code is shown as standard R output:

```{r}
draw(x_ctx, "latex")
```

The additional arguments of the methods have the same meaning as in the text
format. Node information is represented by default in a small table, with the
label of the node on a first row and its frequencies, probabilities or model on
the following one(s):

```{r}
draw(x_ctx, "latex", frequency = "detailed")
```

The names of the states are sanitised to avoid problems induced by LaTeX
special characters:

```{r}
x_special <- sample(c("$1", "a_b", "{c}"), 100, replace = TRUE)
draw(ctx_tree(x_special, max_depth = 1), "latex")
```

### Customising the LaTeX output

The following parameters of `draw_control()` apply to the LaTeX format:

- `tabular`: when `FALSE`, the information attached to a node is given after
  its label, between parentheses, instead of in a table (this parameter is
  ignored by `draw.covlmc()`, which always uses tables);
- `orientation`: `"vertical"` (default) draws the tree from top to bottom,
  while `"horizontal"` draws it from right to left;
- `decoration`: `"none"` (default), `"rectangle"`, `"circle"` or `"ellipse"`
  adds borders of the corresponding shape around all the nodes;
- `fontsize` and `prob_fontsize`: the LaTeX font sizes (such as `"small"` or
  `"large"`) of the labels of the nodes and of the additional information
  (`"normalsize"` and `"small"` by default);
- `digits`: the number of significant digits, as for the text format.

```{r}
draw(elec_vlmc, "latex",
  control = draw_control(
    tabular = FALSE,
    orientation = "horizontal",
    decoration = "rectangle",
    fontsize = "small",
    prob_fontsize = "footnotesize",
    digits = 2
  )
)
```

### VLMC with covariates

The LaTeX representation of a VLMC with covariates differs from its text
counterpart:

- models are always represented with the names of the variables, unless
  `model = NULL` (`"coef"` and `"full"` are equivalent);
- constant models are always represented by the probability distribution they
  induce (`constant_as_prob` is ignored);
- the intercept is denoted `(I)` and the variables are given with a temporal
  subscript of the form $t-1$, $t-2$, etc. They are named after the covariates
  (with the level between square brackets for a factor, as in `y[B]`);
- the coefficients of the levels of a factor that are absent from the data of a
  context, which are not estimated, are represented by zeros, whatever the
  computing engine (in the text format, `VGAM::vglm()` gives no coefficient
  for them, see the article on [computing engines](covlmc-engines.html));
- p-values (with `p_value = TRUE`) are given in parentheses after the labels of
  the nodes.

The `tab_orientation` parameter of `draw_control()` specifies the layout of
the tables that represent the models. By default (`"vertical"`), the variables
are listed in the first column, followed by one column of coefficients per
non-reference state, which is well adapted to models with a long memory of the
covariates. With `with_state = TRUE`, the first row gives the reference state
(above the variables) and the other states (above their coefficients):

```{r}
draw(elec_covlmc, "latex", with_state = TRUE)
```

With `tab_orientation = "horizontal"`, the variables are listed in the first
row, followed by one row of coefficients per non-reference state (the
reference state and the other states are then given in the first column when
`with_state = TRUE`):

```{r}
draw(elec_covlmc, "latex",
  with_state = TRUE,
  control = draw_control(tab_orientation = "horizontal")
)
```

With three states or more, the tables have several columns (or rows) of
coefficients, as illustrated below with a simpler version of the three-state
model used above, whose contexts are limited to a length of one:

```{r}
z_covlmc_1 <- covlmc(z, data.frame(y = y),
  min_size = 1.5, alpha = 0.01, max_depth = 1
)
draw(z_covlmc_1, "latex", with_state = TRUE)
```

### Using the LaTeX code

In a LaTeX document, the code produced by `draw()` can be included as is (for
instance with `\input{}` applied to a file obtained with `writeLines()`, as
shown above), provided the `forest` package is loaded in the preamble of the
document:

```latex
\usepackage{forest}
```

In an R Markdown or Quarto document that produces LaTeX (for instance a PDF
document), no specific step is needed: calling `draw(model, "latex")` in a
chunk is enough to render the tree. Indeed, when the output of the document is
LaTeX, the LaTeX representation is included as is in the document, without the
need for a `results = "asis"` chunk option, and the `forest` package is added
automatically to the preamble. More precisely, the package adds the following
lines to the preamble:

```latex
\usepackage{etoolbox}
\AtEndPreamble{\csname @ifpackageloaded\endcsname{forest}{}{\usepackage{forest}}}
```

The `\AtEndPreamble` command of the `etoolbox` package delays the loading of
`forest` to the end of the preamble, where it is loaded only if the document
has not loaded it already. A document can therefore load `forest` itself,
anywhere in its preamble and possibly with options (such as
`\usepackage[external]{forest}`, to cache the trees), without conflict.

Each tree is included as a paragraph of its own: when a chunk draws several
trees, they are placed one below the other.

In other output formats, such as the HTML format of this article, the LaTeX
representation is shown as standard R output. Finally, notice that text
representations remain available in a document that produces LaTeX. As the
`mixvlmc.charset` option is set when the package is loaded, it is set to
`"ascii"` when the package is loaded while knitting such a document
(`cli::is_utf8_output()` reports that LaTeX output does not support UTF-8
characters).
